utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before you call the next witness, I'd asked you to spend five minutes telling us about the charges in the indictment to which this witness's testimony relates. He's scheduled for I think it is nine hours -- 12 hours, so it would help the Chamber to manage the evidence better, to understand it better, if you gave us a brief outline.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the briefest possible terms, then, Mr. Robinson, in view of the fact that General Stevanovic was the assistant minister of the interior and that he spent time in Kosovo at different intervals, periods and occasions very frequently and that he is well acquainted with the situation and that ex officio he was able to have access to all the relevant information for what we're discussing here. And he is going to testify as extensively as you said, but we're not wasting time. On the contrary, we're making up the time because -- and saving time because he's covering a large number of issues and questions that need to be elucidated and clarified here. In fact, we can say that the testimony of the general is linked to all five counts from 1 to 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counts 1 to 5, that's very general. That's all counts. What about the paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, what I've said is very general, but I'm going to be more specific. And then he will testify, for example when, it comes to paragraphs -- the paragraphs, an important paragraph is paragraph 16 in which -- which talks about joint criminal enterprise and some sort of plan of that joint criminal enterprise, and you'll be seeing documents testifying to the opposite, that is to say measures -- confidence-building measures which cannot be brought into connection with any of this. But the intentions were quite the opposite, quite the reverse, and acts to support that. So as I say, linked to paragraph 16 and 19, where it says that there is responsibility and -- criminal responsibility for the acts or omissions of their subordinates, of the perpetrators, as contained in paragraph 19. So that is another thing linked to a specific count. And then the authorisation and relationship between the army and the police and the subordination-resubordination issue. And then linked to paragraph 23, the functioning and control of the police. Then we go on to paragraph 27, which mentions the Ministry of the Interior and then it is claimed that they committed crimes in counts 1 to 5 in the indictment. And then 28, the crimes of the -- the alleged crimes of the employees of the MUP, as it says in paragraph 28. And then furthermore we come to the link to paragraph 95, which talks about the forces of the FRY and Serbia who started a campaign of shelling on predominantly Albanian towns and villages in Kosovo, et cetera, et cetera. And we're going to give quite clear information as to what was actually happening. And then the extensive use of force, that issue. So those are just some of the things that are linked to this document, in very brief terms, superficial terms. And he is going to testify -- in view of his competence and authority in Kosovo and Metohija, he is going to testify about the situation there itself, the situation in Kosovo and Metohija during the material time when he was there and the joint forces of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija. He's going to testify linked to the paragraphs and counts that I mentioned about the organisation and competence once again of the Ministry of the Interior, and he's going to clarify and elucidate certain questions linked to ranks in the police force because that was the topic of expertise by a group of experts and presented by Mr. Nice, trying to show, as he put it, I believe, that the police was militarised. And you will have an opportunity of getting clear explanations of that. And then the supervision of the police, and then a question that was mentioned quite a lot, Joint Command in Kosovo and Metohija. He's also going to testify about local security matters and a very widespread activity of establishing confidence-building measures and organising the Albanians in the villages to act as a local police force, which is quite contradictory to what Mr. Nice claims with respect to the intentions or, rather, to perpetrate crimes against them and do evil to them. He's going to speaking about the circumstances in which the police worked in Kosovo and Metohija, the legality of the work of the police force. He's going to talk about the events resulting in death which are to be found in the indictment. I haven't listed them here separately, but there are several events of that type to be addressed. And he's going to speak of the sanitation of the terrain that was also mentioned, the refugees and displaced persons that was also a subject of discussion here. We discussed it at length and heard different testimony about that. And also the paramilitary groups and volunteers and the meetings and state policy and politics with respect to what was going on in the region. So there you have it, in the briefest possible terms of breakdown in the several minutes I've taken up about what this witness is going to testify. He's also going to introduce a series of documents through his testimony. As he was on the spot, on location, he'll be able to testify with great competence on all these matters that I have indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. That's informative. Will the testimony follow the structure that you just presented in terms of sequence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly speaking, yes. In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And, Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Stevanovic, where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1953 in Brekovo, the Arilje municipality of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what education have you had?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I completed primary school where I was born in 1969, elementary school, and then the secondary school for internal affairs or secondary police school in Sremska Kamenica near Novi Sad. I completed that in 1973. And the military academy for the ground forces in Belgrade I completed in 1977.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me briefly, please, where you worked and what positions you occupied.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From 1977 until 1979, I worked in the secondary police school in Sremska Kamenica. From 1979 until 2001, I worked in the Republican Secretariat for the Interior, for Internal Affairs or, rather, the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia; and from 2001 to the present day, I've been working at the police academy in Belgrade and I'm there now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, based on what you've just told us, you have spent your entire working career in the police force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been wearing a police uniform since I was 16, and it goes on to the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me briefly, please, what specific tasks did you do in the Republican Secretariat for the Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Republican Secretariat for the Interior or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia I performed a number of different tasks of a medium leadership level and higher leadership level. From 1979, for example, up until 1983, I was the executive officer and leader of the group and then head of department or, rather, sector in the department for law and order, and later on in the police administration. From 1983 until 1990, I was also the head of the sector and head of the department in the police administration; and from 1990 up until 1996, I was also the head of a department in the police administration, then police commander, then deputy head of the police administration and the head of the police administration after that. From mid-1997 up until the beginning of the year 2000 or, rather, 2001, I was assistant minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, who appoints assistant ministers of the interior to that post?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: All the assistant ministers in the government of the Republic of Serbia are appointed by the government of Serbia as well as the assistant ministers in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that I don't need to explain who appoints the ministers themselves.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, of course. All the ministers are elected by the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us the criteria for the selection of assistant ministers. How -- what is the criteria like for that selection?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Ministry of the Interior, all the assistant ministers since I've been working in the Ministry of the Interior were appointed according to their professional criteria and not their political criteria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, when the government appoints an assistant minister, does it also assign and determine their authorisations?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The government just appoints the assistant minister to the post of minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who determines the assignments?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The assignments specifically of the assistant minister, since there are several ministers in the Ministry of the Interior and there were six during my time in the ministry, is determined by the minister of the interior himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does each of the assistant ministers of the interior, are they at the head of a particular branch or department of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Ministry of the Interior, no, because during my period in the ministry or, rather, when I was there, there were two basic sectors, sections -- sectors, and there were six assistant ministers. So the minister decides and determines which of those six assistant ministers would head one of the two sectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of work did you do predominantly in your professional career? What were your assignments and tasks as assistant minister? What did that include?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, while working in the Ministry of the Interior, I generally dealt with organisational matters, normative matters, and other professional subjects and matters relating to the selection, training, and equipment of police cadres of general purpose. While I was assistant minister, pursuant to a decision of the minister I was more specifically in charge of affairs from the realm of the police administration, the operative centre of the Ministry of the Interior, and also for education institutions and training institutions within the Ministry of the Interior; that is to say, the police academy, the higher school of the interior, and secondary school for the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 4, can we find, inter alia, an excerpt from the law on state administration of the Republic of Serbia. There are excerpts from different laws here. This particular one says how assistant ministers are appointed and what kind of work they do and what they do within their job description in terms of what the minister gives them as an assignment. Is that contained in this tab?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is part of the law on the organisation of state administration, but unfortunately I haven't got the opportunity to see that particular tab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I hope that you have all the tabs right next to you on that shelf. So please use them. You have the right to use all documents that were given to everyone else in this room. Let's not waste time. There's a direct quotation here of Article 46 from this law just as you mentioned, and that's contained in this quotation. Is that exactly what you established just now, General?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is Article 46 of the law on state administration of the Republic of Serbia, which clearly states who appoints assistant ministers and what their line of work is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. In tab 9, we have this document of the minister or, rather, the minister's dispatch dated the 4th of June, 1997. I'm going to skip everything that does not pertain to you since this is a general document that has to do with the duties of assistant ministers. Here it says General -- Major General Obrad Stevanovic for administration of the police and operative centre for the schools of the interior and the police academy. So that was contained in the dispatch, in this information that was sent to everybody in the ministry. Does this compass your scope of work? That is to say, police administration, the operative centre, the secondary and higher schools of the interior, and the police academy.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's schooling, and you referred to that.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. This is a document, a decision of the minister of the interior informing the entire ministry and all its units that I was appointed assistant minister and also what duties he assigned to me. And of course not only to me but also to other assistant ministers at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I assume that I can ask for all these tabs to be admitted into evidence later because this is just documentation corroborating what the witness has been saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you can ask. What are the duties that were assigned to him? It's not translated, is it? I'd like to find out the duties that were assigned to him. So could it be placed on the ELMO, and could you direct us to the passages, if there are any, which indicate the duties that were assigned to him. But let us give a number for the binder. It's 2 -- 299.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's tab number 9. I hope it's on the ELMO now. In the one but last paragraph, the one but last paragraph that has to do with Major General Obrad Stevanovic, it says: "Major General Obrad Stevanovic for affairs related to the police administration and operative centre, for the secondary and higher School of Internal Affairs and the police academy." All the other paragraphs pertain to the other assistant ministers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in which period were you in Kosovo and Metohija on official business?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From 1981 until 1999, I went on official business to Kosovo and Metohija, every now and then on official business. So that is to say almost 18 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a well-known thing that the Ministry of the Interior, the Republican Secretariat of the Interior, as it was called at the time until the constitutional amendments were passed in 1989, did not really have any powers in the autonomous provinces, the autonomous provinces that were a part of Serbia. How come you were in Kosovo and Metohija on official business from 1981 until 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, what you asserted previously is correct; that is to say the Republican Secretariat of the Interior practically at that time did not have any powers in the territory of the autonomous provinces. I stayed on official business in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija at that time within the command of the joint forces of the Federal Secretariat of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These joint forces of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior came from all republics; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Within these joint forces of the police of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior there were police units from all the republics of the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your duties in Kosovo and Metohija after 1989?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: After 1989, primarily in the period from 1989 to 1990 and perhaps up to 1991, I was in Kosovo and Metohija within the staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija, and in that period I was head of that staff at least on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these accusations that were brought here there are references made to 1988 and 1989 primarily. Tell me, at that time were you in Kosovo on official business? I'm talking about '88 and '89.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During 1988 and during 1989, I was often in Kosovo and Metohija, and always upon instructions from the minister in order to do what the minister of the interior at the time had instructed us to do. For the most part, this work of mine had to do with the following: Together with leaders of organisational units of the police in Kosovo and Metohija in the staff for Kosovo and Metohija, I was supposed to have meetings together with all of them, and at such meetings I was supposed to convey the positions, the instructions, and the assignments given by the minister, to see to what extent these tasks were carried out, and then to brief him on what had been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the tasks that you had with a view to the implementation of the agreement of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the Kosovo Verification Mission, first and foremost in Belgrade in the second half of 1998, I was a member of the official delegation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia at the talks with the representatives of NATO that were headed by Generals Clark and Naumann. At that meeting, what was primarily discussed were measures for implementing the agreement on the Verification Mission, specifically on reducing police troops in Kosovo and Metohija and especially reducing the scope of work of the police in Kosovo and Metohija. After that meeting in Belgrade, I went to Kosovo and Metohija in order to work on the implementation of the agreement of the Kosovo Verification Mission and the document that was signed by Schombers [phoen] and General Djordjevic after the meeting in Belgrade. And then I was supposed to look at this with the top personnel in Kosovo and Metohija in order to prepare them for the implementation of this agreement. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it is clear enough. I just want to get the questions in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right order, so I need to mark some things on this paper that I have here. So just a second, please. Now, in addition to the fact that over a long period of time you held top positions in the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and in Kosovo and Metohija, as one of the top people in the Ministry of the Interior, in what other ways did you receive information about what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As assistant minister, and before that as deputy head of the police administration and head of the police administration, I was informed every day about security events in the territory of the republic, especially what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija. Also, I often had occasion to attend important meetings where there were discussions on the security situation in the Republic of Serbia, notably the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. As for everything that was going on and all the measures that were taken in Kosovo and Metohija, my knowledge is based on my own state in Kosovo and Metohija, the work I did there myself, my presence at meetings, important meetings at that, where the subject matter was discussed, and also daily and periodical information received on the security situation in the republic, especially in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During one of your previous answers, General, you explained that you were in Kosovo and Metohija for quite a long period of time. Of course not all the time, but from 1981 until mid-1999. I would like to put a question to you: Security related problems in Kosovo and Metohija throughout that period, from 1981 to 1999, were they always of the same degree of complexity and intensity?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was quite clear that the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija became more complex and then was alleviated in cycles. A particularly complex situation in Kosovo and Metohija reigned from 1981 to 1983, and then from 1989 to 1990, and of course the most complex situation started in 1998 and 1999. Perhaps I could add one more thing because I omitted to mention that in relation to my activities in Kosovo; that in mid-June, as a member of the delegation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and of the Republic of Serbia, I attended the talks on establishing the peace in Kosovo, and I'm the signatory of the Kumanovo agreement on behalf of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that, General.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I thought that I had omitted an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you mean in relation to your own activities.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How and in which way did this first cycle of violence in Kosovo and Metohija start, to the best of your knowledge? We're talking about your knowledge. I'm not asking you about the '60, '65, '68, whatever, only your own knowledge at the time when you were there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. My knowledge dates back to the time when I joined the Ministry of the Interior, and I already said that I first stayed in Kosovo and Metohija in 1981. So my first professional knowledge about what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija dates back to that period, that is to say 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in this year 1981? What was characteristic of that year?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 1981 is characteristic because there were sudden violent demonstrations staged by Albanians first in Pristina and then throughout Kosovo and Metohija, and of course the consequences of that violence. Very often there were deaths as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the key demand of these violent demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a generally known fact, and the demonstrators were not concealing that fact either: Kosovo Republic. That was the main slogan, and it was present everywhere and all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were there yourself, and you say Kosovo Republika, now Kosovo Republic. When Professor Slavenko Terzic testified here, Mr. Nice suggested to him that these were student revolts that had to do with the poor quality of food. Was that the reason or only what you said just now?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course that was no reason. It was evident to all who were there and I believe all who could follow these demonstrations in the media. The alleged problem of poor quality food was just used as a pretext for guising the separatist nature of the demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you said that tensions went up and down and that there were tensions on the rise. One of these cycles was in the late '80s and the beginning of the '90s and within about one year, a year and a half. What were the activities of the Albanian separatists, the Albanian separatist movement at that time?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, as opposed to 1981, it was somewhat different. When I say "different," I mean special forms of expressing their political motives and special forms of disguising the political motives and objectives of these demonstrations. I remember very well, first and foremost, this so calmed uni-ethnic poisoning. I remember the exceptional activities in settling alleged blood feuds between different families. I remember the protests of the Trepca miners in the mines. Of course, I was also present when the illegal Assembly was held in Pristina. And, of course, I remember when the illegal constitution was adopted in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall from that period any particular event or events or any type of behaviour that resulted in the departure of Albanian policemen from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. I myself took part in attempts made to overcome this problem. That is to say, most of the policemen who were ethnic Albanians at that time, on orders issued by the separatist movement, decided to leave the police force, and the Ministry of the Interior at the time did their best to convince people that there was no reason to do that. However, all efforts made to keep the Albanian policemen within the police force of the Republic of Serbia practically did not succeed. I myself was present at a few gatherings of policemen, and I conducted long exhaustive detailed discussions, convincing them that they were citizens of the Republic of Serbia, that they were policemen of the Republic of Serbia, and that there is not a single reason for them to leave the police. Of course, all these attempts did not bear any fruit. It was obvious that they had political instructions to do that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally talk to a great number of Albanian policemen about this?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. First of all, I talked in the municipal hall of Gnjilane with over 200 Albanian policemen for over three hours, at least. All the policemen were then armed. Some even had long barrels. If I remember well, the meeting was attended by General Lukic. He is a general now, I don't remember his rank at the time. We did all we could, but we did not succeed in convincing them that there was no reason whatsoever for them to leave the police and that it was in our common interest for them to stay on the force, considering that Albanians in the Kosovo police were a majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that everybody in this hall was armed, everybody had their sidearms at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any incidents? Was there any unrest at this meeting during the discussions?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no unrest or incidents in connection with this. I went to Pristina for the same purpose several times, and if I remember well, I went to Kosovska Mitrovica as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of them state their reasons for leaving the police force? You said the meeting in Gnjilane alone lasted three hours. What were they saying about their reasons?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had many former schoolmates among Albanians from the higher school for internal affairs from Sremska Kamenica and from the academy of the ground forces in Belgrade, and I asked my former schoolmates what was going on, and the only thing they were able to tell me was, "We must do this. We have to do this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What year is this? 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was 1989 or maybe 1990. I cannot be quite sure. But this is a matter of common knowledge. I cannot place it exactly within a year, but it was one of those two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will not now go back to quote these allegations, because everybody in this courtroom knows them, but do you know from that time - let's take 1990 - about anything -- about any case of dismissal of Albanian policemen from the organs of internal affairs in the province of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge, and I'm absolutely certain that there were no such attempts and no such decisions. On the contrary, great efforts were made to keep Albanian policemen on the force in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many Albanian policemen remained in Kosovo and Metohija working on the force after this desertion that you described?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Despite this general desertion of the police force by Albanian policemen, a certain number of policemen remained on the force. I cannot remember the exact number, but if I remember correctly, 4 per cent of the total troops remained. Of course, all those who had left had to be replaced, so that additional police units were sent to Kosovo to replace those who had left in order for the police to continue to be able to discharge their regular duties related to public law and order, traffic safety, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the constitutional obligation of the Republic of Serbia to protect the rights and freedoms of all its citizens?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Doubtlessly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that organs of internal affairs play an important role in the protection of those rights and freedoms?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Indubitably. Organs of internal affairs had a very important role in the protection of rights and freedoms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already mentioned that organs of internal affairs of Serbia had no powers in Kosovo and Metohija until the constitutional amendments in 1989. Tell me, why were the joint forces of the Federal Secretariat of Internal Affairs established?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The joint forces of the Federal Secretariat of Internal Affairs were established at the time as the only way to restore peace and order to Kosovo and Metohija in the general situation when security and public law and order were in jeopardy. And as I have already said, the police of Serbia could not play that role because the authorities of the province were against the Serbian police entering the province. I remember very clearly that the police units that had been placed on alert in order to restore peace and order in Kosovo after the demonstrations I described waited at the administrative border of Kosovo in Rasko, Kursumlija, Vranje for over seven days, but they were not allowed to go in. And following certain political activities, it was decided eventually that only forces under the command of the then Federal Secretariat of Internal Affairs would be allowed to go in. That was the situation from the demonstrations in 1981 until 1989. Only the forces of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior were allowed to go into Kosovo. These forces were made up of police troops from all over Yugoslavia. I can tell you where the forces from each republic were mainly concentrated if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not necessary. Tell me, who was the federal secretary of the interior and who was the federal Prime Minister at the time when these joint federal forces existed in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, and I think I do -- I'm sure, in fact. In 1981, the Federal Secretariat of the Interior was General Franko Herljevic, Franjo Herljevic. I believe the federal Prime Minister was Stane Dolanc. And after him, it was Dobrosav Culafic. Sorry, the following ministers were Stane Dolanc, and Dobrosav Culafic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were the federal Prime Ministers?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was first Milka Planinc, and then Branko Mikulic, and after him, Ante Markovic. I think that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these persons that you enumerated, both in the position on the federal minister of the interior and in the position of federal Prime Minister were persons who were not Serbs. In other words, people coming from other republics of the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. None of the persons I enumerated were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in command of these joint federal forces to which you belonged?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Senior leaders from the Federal Secretariat of the Interior and the police brigade of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior were in command, such as Brigade Commander Slavko Strika, then Special Purpose Battalion Commander Franc Kosi, and several other leaders whose names I cannot recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, General. I think this will suffice. This covers this entire period from 1981 to 1989 when the joint forces of the federal police were involved in Kosovo and Metohija. General, one of the witnesses who have appeared here, an expert witness who was called to explain the work of the police, claimed that Serbia was a police state and that the police force in Serbia was a politicised and militarised force. In view of your position and your knowledge about the subject, your personal involvement and the positions you occupied, I will now ask you a series of questions regarding the structure and organisation of the police in order for everybody to understand these things clearly. Tell me, during the '90s in Serbia, is it the case that there was one single Secretariat of the Interior, a unified single Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period up to 1990, in the Republic of Serbia there was one single Ministry of the Interior that was in charge of the entire republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about before the constitutional amendments?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the constitutional amendments in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, there was one Republican Secretariat for the Interior and two provincial secretariats that were completely independent of the Republican Secretariat of the Interior, so that the republican SUP had powers practically only in the territory of central Serbia but not in the territory of the autonomous provinces which were part of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in the course of 1970s, was the ministry -- excuse me, 1990s, was it a centralised ministry or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second. The answer that you gave previously, "In that period up to 1990..." should that have been after 1990 or is it up to 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, which answer do you mean? One of my answers related to the period prior to 1990, and the other answer after 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll read the answer and you can tell me what is correct. "In that period up to 1990, in the Republic of Serbia, there was one single Ministry of the Interior that was in charge of the entire republic." Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a mistake. That should refer to the period after 1990. One single ministry in charge of the territory of the entire republic existed after 1990, not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what the witness actually said at the time, after 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have clarified this, General. Since there was one ministry, in organisational terms it means it was centralised.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: But I haven't completed my answer, sorry. In the period after 1990, in the republic of the whole Republic of Serbia, there was one ministry in charge of all the affairs prescribed by the law as belonging to this ministry for the entire Serbia. Organisationally speaking, of course it was centralised. However, functionally speaking, one could say that the Ministry of the Interior was decentralised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean in practical terms? It's not clear enough.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This functional decentralisation within a centralised ministry means practically that in keeping with the law on internal affairs as well as other legislation, the vehicle of police powers is the authorised officer. In other words, a policeman. So it is the policeman who is empowered and not the ministry. Apart from that, lower organisational units in municipalities are also in keeping with the law responsible for the security situation on the territory of their municipalities. So to summarise, the ministry was centralised in organisational terms. However, specific duties were discharged by authorised officers, that is policemen and the authorities in municipalities, and they are the vehicles of police power in municipalities and responsible for the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which legislation stipulates the powers of the MUP in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The affairs that belong within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior are specified by the law which is practically changed with each new government. These affairs used to be stipulated by Article 7 of the then law on ministries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in tab 4 where we have excerpts from these various pieces of legislation, we have also an excerpt that relates to the Ministry of the Interior. Would you please read it. That is precisely Article 7 on the law on the ministries of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Article 7 of the law on the ministries of the Republic of Serbia defines matters within the purview of the ministry and says: "The Ministry of the Interior shall attend to matters of state administration relating to the following: "Protecting the security of the Republic of Serbia and detecting and preventing activities aimed at undermining or destroying the constitutionally established order. "Protecting lives and guaranteeing personal safety and the security of citizens' property. "Preventing and detecting crimes, finding and apprehending perpetrators and bringing them before the competent organs. "Maintaining public law and order. "Providing security at rallies and other public gatherings. "Providing security for specific officials and buildings. "Road traffic safety. "Monitoring crossings of the state border. "Monitoring movement and presence in the border belt. "Monitoring movement and presence of foreigners. "Procurement, possession, and carrying of weapons and ammunition. "Production and sale of explosives, flammable liquids and gases. "Fire-fighting. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "Citizenship, personal identification number, personal identity cards, passports, citizens' domicile and place of residence. "Training personnel and other matters prescribed by law." That is Article 7 of the law on the ministries of the Republic of Serbia that was in force at the time. It must have been amended in the meantime, but we can conclude from this that the purview of the Ministry of the Interior was such that it can be divided into police affairs and internal administration affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, what organisational wholes and entities was the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia compiled?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: After 1990, in the organisational sense, the Ministry of the Interior changed relatively slightly up until 1999, and within the ministry there were two sectors, the sector of state security and the sector of public security. The public security sector had organisational entities at the seat of the ministry and territorial units as well. I don't know whether you want me to go into detail here and give you a further breakdown of those units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what the territorial units were.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The territorial organisational units were the secretariats of the interior which performed duties from the purview of the ministry as contained in the former article mentioned in the districts of Serbia and the districts were in fact administrative units, how the territory was divided up in administrative terms. And within the secretariat, the organisational units in charge of the municipalities and the territory there were the departments of the interior or police stations in the smaller municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can we see what this looks like on the basis of the law governing the Ministry of the Interior that we find in tab 5? It's rather a long document. I don't want to dwell on it for too long.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In fact, this document is the rules. Not the law but the rules, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Article 1, if you found that, the organisational units of the ministry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I observe it's not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, we have the advantage with this witness, in terms of documents, that almost all of them have been translated. However, the entire rules I -- we considered would be irrational to translate the entire rules which are given here as an exhibit. We have the entire text here in the original. But I merely wish to dwell on the establishment of the organisational aspects, which can be seen on the basis of these rules and which relate to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To what sections do you wish to refer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we look at Article 3, for example, we will find a list of the organisational units, and it says the secretariats in the text to follow, and they start out with Belgrade. Article 3.1 is Belgrade. They're not grouped for Kosovo and Metohija, but under number 5 we will find Gnjilane for the municipalities of VP Gnjilane, Kosovska Kamenica and Novo Brdo. 6 is Djakovica, for the municipalities of Djakovica and Decani. Number 11 is Kosovska Mitrovica, the Secretariat of the Interior for the municipalities of Vucitrn, Svec [phoen], Zubin Potok, Kosovska Mitrovica, Leposavic and Srbica. Number 20 is Pec, for the municipalities of Istok, Glina and Pec. Number 23 is Prizren, for the municipalities of Gora, Opolje, Orahovac, Prizren, and Suva Reka. Number 24 is Pristina, for the municipalities Glogovac, Kosovo Polje, Lipljan, Obilic, Podujevo and Pristina. Number 31 is Urosevac, the secretariat for that, for the municipalities of Kacanik, Urosevac, Stimlje and Strpce. On several occasions here we came across these names, place names and places mentioned here, so it is a good idea for us to see how the service of the interior or Ministry of the Interior was organised in those particular municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you're going to rely extensively on it, that will not be possible. I won't allow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I won't be relying on the document extensively. I just wanted to highlight a couple of points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that is what you've already done. You can just ask the witness whether what you have read out confirms the organisational structure, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I read out the Secretariats of the Interior and the composition in Kosovo. Is that the organisational structure? Does that confirm it in the way in which you have explained it to us?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You've read out the Secretariats of the Interior that were set up for the area of Kosovo and Metohija in such a way as to define the municipalities which come under their competence in security related terms. And I could just add to that that the duties and affairs pursuant to the law were determined by the law and that the organisation of the ministry was determined by the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the rules contained in tab 5?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what types of police units existed within the frameworks of the public security sector, that is to say the uniformed police sector?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, within the public security sector there were different units in the general sense. There was the crime unit, general unit, traffic safety unit, border belt unit, intervention unit, and so on and so forth. Within the uniformed police, when we say "uniformed police" we have in mind the general police units first and foremost of general competence and authority, then traffic police units, then border police units, and finally the so-called police intervention units or, rather, police units -- Special Purpose Units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Special Purpose Units. I see. So that is the PJP abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the relevant time, and we're talking about 1998 and 1999 here, how many policemen did Serbia have, the total number of policemen?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the last decade of the 20th century or, rather, in the 1990s in the Republic of Serbia, the total number of policemen were approximately 25.000 policemen, plus or minus 1 to 2 per cent, of course. Out of a total of 37.000 employees working in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you explained to us a moment ago, I believe, what we mean when we say an authorised official pursuant to the law and as stipulated by the law. So when you say 37.000 employees, MUP employees, the 25.000, are those those authorised persons, authorised officers?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 25.000 are authorised officers or persons; that is, in simple terms, the policemen, policemen with police authorisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the 12.000? The difference between 25.000 and 37.000, what is the 12.000?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were the administrative staff, the administrative employees and also the fire brigade. We had the fire brigade units and in Serbia those come under the Ministry of the Interior, the firefighters. Then we have the various personnel department employees, logistics, et cetera, administrative department, financial department, and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the kitchens to the fire brigades; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the kitchens to the fire brigades

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, so those are all the units that come under the Ministry of the Interior, and you said 25.000 policemen in all, in total. Now, what is the per capita ratio of policemen and citizens in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we analysed the ratio between the number of citizens and the number of policemen in the republic and tried to compare that to other countries because individuals sometimes said that there were too many policemen. I remember full well when it was quite obvious that in Serbia for every policeman there were 400 citizens -- or the other way round. It was a 400 to 1 ratio. And if you look at 10.000 inhabitants, then it would be 2.5 policemen per 1.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, since you're comparing -- you said you compared the figure to other countries, who did you compare our country to?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember looking at France, the figures for France, for example, according to our figures, that there were five policemen to every 1.000 inhabitants and that was 4. something. As far as I remember in Czechoslovakia, for example, about 4.5, and in Croatia 4.5. In Belgium it is 3.5. So from those figures, we were closer to Great Britain where it was 250 -- 2.5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in most European countries - you've mentioned some of them - do they have local police forces or communal municipal police forces that doesn't -- that -- whose figure doesn't figure in the overall figure?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in -- with the statistics, we had two problems. There are different definitions defining a policeman in the different countries. Not all countries define a policeman the same way. Some states have decentralised police forces, so they have a state police force and a local police force, for example. In the Republic of Serbia, from what I've said so far it is quite clear that each and every policeman was a state policeman, if I can put it that way, and every policeman is counted within the statistical analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you mean is there were no other policemen apart from the 25.000 policemen or authorised officers in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we felt that in other countries, the local policemen were not included into those general statistics, just the state policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I hope that that ratio is clear now in comparison to other countries as well and within our own country and figures are easily comparable. Now, tell me, General, from your own experience, for example, in the leadership post that you occupied in the ministry and your general experience in your many years of service in the police force, what criteria were used to select the leadership cadres in the police force of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question in part already. Throughout my time in the police force, especially since I was in the assistant minister, which is 1996 and 1997, and after that date I claim that the key, main, and sole criteria applied for the selection of the leadership cadre in the police were professional criteria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's pause there for a moment. You were assistant minister. Were you in a situation -- or, rather, did you personally propose certain individuals, leaders to the minister from the force to assume certain positions within the ministry?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that comes within the purview of an assistant minister. The proposal of cadres, putting forward names, nominating people for different positions and levels within the ministry. And this was of course something that all the assistant ministers did, not only I myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, I'm interested in the following: Since you were in a position to put forward candidates and give your opinion, take your own example. Did you ask any candidate for his political options or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. None of the candidates that I put forward did I ever ask to which political -- which political options they held. And let me also say that the minister never asked me. The only important thing for me was what the man was like, what his professional capabilities were like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine, General, thank you. Now, tell us what the organisational structure was like of the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija itself.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The organisational structure?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everything that existed. I want to know everything that came under the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija or any people under the ministry spending time in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, the organisational structure, the organisational units of the ministry in Kosovo and Metohija did not differ in any way from the organisational structure of the ministry, for example, in Vojvodina province or in Sumadija or anywhere else in Serbia. So all the Secretariats of the Interior were organised in exactly the same way; they had the same structure, they had the same purview, the same competencies and authority. The numerical state and the number of internal organisational units depended on the territory covered by a secretariat and the security related situation in the given area. Now, of course, if you're asking me about the period from 1998 and 1999, then what I can say is this: There were certain additions to what I've just said. In addition to the regular police units, there were extraordinary local units and units sent there from other secretariats outside Kosovo and Metohija. And I can go into the details if need be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me ask you this: You've told us that the regular forces were the same as in any other part and region of Serbia and from time to time there would be extraordinary units. What kind of units would they be and what functions would they perform?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I can explain that. The regular units in Kosovo were the secretariats for the districts as administrative parts of the territory, then the departments at the level of the municipalities and police stations in the very small areas, smaller than municipalities, et cetera, the communities. So that was how the police stations of general purpose were organised as well. In addition to the general purpose units, the regular units of the police force in Kosovo were the units of the traffic police, mostly in the headquarters of the secretariats, the seven secretariats that we enumerated or, rather, I enumerated in response to another question of yours, and I can say there were four other units, four other border police stations as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Those four were in the tab we saw and the breakdown. They were in Brgovnice [phoen], Djeneral Jankovic, Doganovici [phoen], Pristina, I believe.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Dzapra Krusi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Dzapra Krusi.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I think there were four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Pristina was the airport, the border crossing was the airport. The rest were along the border crossing on land.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Right, and of course in Kosovo the special anti-terrorist unit was located with its permanent headquarters in Pristina and the organisational units belonging to the state security sector. Those were the regular organised units of the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija or, rather, organisational units. Now, in addition to that, in Kosovo and Metohija during 1998 and 1999, there were extraordinary local police units that were engaged, and those first and foremost were the -- were temporary police departments, reserve police departments, local special police units and local reserve force police units. And to round off that answer, the third structure located there were the extraordinary special units sent to Kosovo from other parts of the republic. And when I say that, I mean special units, special police units like a special terrorist unit and the JSO police unit from the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, just one question on that: These extraordinary or additional units, were they comprised entirely of Serb police officers or Serb personnel, or were there Kosovo Albanians as part of any of these groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like us to be very precise on this. I said that there were two groups of extraordinary units, one group established at local level and the units on the other hand that were sent from the other parts of the republic. These units that were sent from the other parts of the republic practically had the kind of manpower that the police in the area that they were being sent from had. In Kosovo and Metohija, the local extraordinary forces also matched the manpower in the area from which they were formed, but it is correct that there were less Albanians within their ranks, significantly less.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that the microphone wasn't turned on and at line 10.20.29 the term was special anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that there were Albanians in the units but I cannot give you any specific names now. I can say, for example, that at the headquarters of the MUP in Kosovo in 1998 and in 1999 - General Sreten Lukic headed that - there was a high ranking Albanian who held a high rank until 1999, all the way up 'til 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the situation in the entire republic, and especially what General Stevanovic said just now about the organisational units, could you please briefly place on the overhead projector this map which is contained in tab 453. There is nothing to be translated here. The secretariats are marked in red, and you can see all the departments and the distribution pattern throughout the territory of Serbia. Please take this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tabs of this number haven't yet been presented to us. We don't -- I think we've got four volumes so far of a projected dozen or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is this tab among the documents that you have presented?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your index ends at 449.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then probably this is an index that was not updated, because this tab does bear the number that I read out. I haven't got it in my hands now, but you can just cast a glance at it. It's very easy to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's look at it, yes. We'll allow that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, in answer to the question. What's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is whether this is a map of the Republic of Serbia with the heads -- with the headquarters of the secretariats marked and all the departments of the interior and their distribution pattern in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. This is a sketch of the division of the territory of the Republic of Serbia according to secretariats and headquarters of the interior. I know that very well that there are 33 such secretariats in the territory of Serbia, four of which are in Kosovo and Metohija -- I'm sorry, seven. Seven are in Kosovo and Metohija. Those are the ones that we mentioned in response to one of the previous questions. On this map, we can also see the municipal organisational units or, rather, the units of the Ministry of the Interior in the territories of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the entire organisational structure can be seen on this map.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. The territorial horizontal review of the Ministry of the Interior in the 1990s. And I believe that it has remained unchanged until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What were the assignments given to the police Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forces and how many forces were there in Kosovo and Metohija, how many police personnel?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The police forces in Kosovo and Metohija were primarily engaged in carrying out their every day regular policework, that is to say protecting law and order and the safety and security of citizens and institutions in Kosovo and Metohija. Of course, in the period of 1998 and 1999, one of the key priority tasks was to combat terrorism. In addition to that, another important task was to prevent all forms of serious crime, organised crime, drug smuggling, weapon smuggling, and so on. That is to say, control of terrorism and control of serious crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As for all this work, is this regulated in the law on the interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Everything that the police did in Kosovo they did in accordance with the law on internal affairs and of course other laws that the police apply in their work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these laws -- as for this particular law, Mr. Robinson, it is in tab 1. It is there. It is an excerpt from the Official Gazette. As for the other regulations, I've already quoted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I asked you about the number of personnel in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The figures in terms of the police in Kosovo and Metohija, are they contained in tab 13?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is an overview of police levels in Kosovo and Metohija at one particular point in time, specifically the 4th of June, 1999. This survey shows the local forces - that's the first five vertical columns - and also the forces that were seconded there in the following five columns. And in the last vertical column on the right we see the total number of police in Kosovo and Metohija at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This has to do with the state of war; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The total level of police presence in Kosovo and Metohija during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it is logical that that is when the police presence peaked in Kosovo and Metohija. And I know full well that there were never more than 16.000 policemen in Kosovo and Metohija. That is the maximum number that ever appeared in Kosovo and Metohija. This survey shows this maximum police presence in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted this survey to be admitted precisely for that reason, because that shows the maximum strength. I wanted to ask you whether there could have been more than this, but you said that this was the maximum number that could be found in Kosovo and Metohija during the war.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This was the maximum number that actually was in Kosovo and Metohija. There could have been more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about what could have happened, whether more could have been sent, but this is the maximum number of policemen that were actually there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear the explanation as to Intervention Brigade and AS and RS. What do they mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please help me with this? Were can these letters be seen? Ah, yes, I can see it now. It is vertical column 5 and vertical column 6. "AS" is an abbreviation for active force, that is to say regular policemen from the Ministry of Interior. "RS" is reserve force, the reserve force of the police. In accordance with the law on internal affairs, it can be engaged in carrying out police work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could explain to me column 3 and 4 as well, which is belonging to 124th Intervention Brigade, PJP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Columns 3 and 4 pertain to the Intervention Brigade of the special police units, and this is a special unit of the police established from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. That is to say there were several special units but this particular unit bearing this number is the local PJP in Kosovo and Metohija. That is to say it is manned only by policemen from the seven secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can I take it that while PJP is a local force, JSO and SAJ [Realtime transcript read in error "ASJ"] is dispatched from Serbia? So they are not local organisations, JSO and SAJ. It's 8th and 9th row in that chart. Transcript should say "SAJ."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot find it. Unfortunately, in columns 8 and 9 I cannot see these abbreviations but of course I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 8th and 9th row. The 8th and 9th line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. I'm sorry I didn't look at this properly. It is quite clear that JSO cannot be a local police unit. That is a state security unit, the JSO, and it is certain that its headquarters were outside Kosovo and Metohija. SAJ, of course, is the special anti-terrorist unit. For the most part it is outside Kosovo and Metohija but part of it is in Kosovo and Metohija. I assume that the entire personnel of that unit is included in column 9 although part of it is not based in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we are going to dwell on these special police units a bit longer but before I move on to this question of special police units, I wanted to deal with this other aspects too that Mr. Nice's expert Babovic presented as proof of militarisation. The first aspect was the actual number that we've already looked at, and we see what that is and we see what the distribution pattern is. Another aspect that he took into account was the existence of ranks in the police. He said that that was an indicator of police militarisation. Please, as a police general and assistant minister, what can you say about that statement?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the entirety of my experience and everything I know, it is obvious that such a statement is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you something? Mr. Babovic is a policeologist. You are a police professional. You teach at the police academy. As a police professional, are you aware of this kind of profession?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know the name. I know the man's name, of course, but I've never actually met him. And I don't know what his career has been. What he called himself from a professional or educational point of view is really a laughing matter as far as police are concerned, because nowhere in the world or, rather, nowhere in any law has such a profile been established. People who graduate from the police academy become graduated police officers. I don't know what kind of school he completed, but I'm quite certain that at that time there was no institution of higher learning in Serbia that schooled such people. I'm quite certain that something like that does not exist in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, you teach at the police academy. You're not a policeologist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. If Mr. Babovic were a policeologist, then in Serbia we'd have 30.000 policeologists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You would be well served. On that note we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can the existence of ranks in the police be used as an argument to claim that the police in Serbia was militarised, a claim made by Mr. Babovic, for instance?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course that is a wrong conclusion. It can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us take it from south to north, east, west. Are there any ranks in the police in Greece, Hungary, France, other countries?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there are ranks in the police in Greece, in France, in Hungary. That should be enough to prove that this claim does not stand up to scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you get the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1996 when I was head of police administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis does one get ranks in police in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the law on ranks for employees of the Ministry of the Interior, the basic criterion for being awarded a rank are professional training, professional experience, time spent in the previous rank, and the requirements for the next rank. So a rank testifies to the professional abilities and competencies and qualifications of a person in view of the rank that he or she is holding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 3, we have the law on ranks, General. Can you please have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have found the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the last paragraph of Article 5. It says: "By completing the basic studies of the police academy, cadets, in keeping with the law, obtain the initial rank of 2nd lieutenant".

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is prescribed by the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on Article 7, because I asked you a moment ago on what basis does one get awarded a rank. It says: "An authorised officer --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... mislaid it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was just observing this. Mr. Milosevic, there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the witness has been reading from Article 5 and it's the last paragraph, I think it would be helpful if it's on the overhead projector so we can see what it is he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we see from this last paragraph of Article 5 that I quoted -- this is a photocopy of the Official Gazette, a publication where legislation is promulgated. It says: "By graduating from the basic course of studies at the police academy, cadets, in keeping with the law, are awarded the initial rank of 2nd lieutenant."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us about Article 7.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It prescribes precisely what I mentioned in my previous answer. "An authorised officer is promoted to the next rank under the following conditions: 1, that he has adequate professional training; 2, that the rank is prescribed for the workplace to which he is assigned or to which he shall be assigned; 3 -- that is again item 2, that a rank is prescribed for the workplace to which the person is assigned or shall be assigned; 3, that he has spent a certain period of time in the previous rank; 4, that he has had positive professional assessment -- performance assessment for the previous two years prior to promotion." Those are the conditions under which one can be promoted to the next rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the relationship between the rank and workplace in the police?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, the rank tells us more about the professional abilities and qualifications for the performance of complex duties, whereas the workplace defines the duties and competencies and powers. The difference is that getting a rank does not add to the rights or authorisations of a person, whereas being assigned to a particular workplace means new rights or authorisations or powers, or maybe losing them. Under the law, a junior corporal, that is a corporal, has the same powers as a person in a higher rank in the same workplace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, was the Prosecution evidence that the force was -- the police force was militarised because it had ranks?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is a part of the case that the creation of ranks reflected the militarisation of the police. The court should obviously -- not "should obviously"; might wish to turn to Mr. Babovic's report at some stage between now and the conclusion of this witness's evidence to understand the nature of the disagreement between the two sides. Certainly, yes, ranks reflect [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were there other factors?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There has been mention of the role of the president of the republic, which is regulated by the law. In this specific case it was my role at the time when I was president of the republic. Do presidents of the republic appoint and assign ranks to members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the republic, of course, never appointed or assigned any member of the Ministry of the Interior. Ranks can be awarded only by authorised officers in the rank of general. So the president of the republic only appoints generals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he appoint generals independently or at somebody's proposal?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the proposal of the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
