utterances.text: Were there any instances when the president of the republic promoted somebody into a higher rank contrary to the proposal of the minister?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know all about promotions, specifically promotions to the rank of general, and I don't think it ever happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So apart from the number, powers, ranks, everything that was used as an argument to claim that the police was allegedly militarised, I will ask you now about the level of arming of the police. Were the level of arming and equipment of the Ministry of the Interior indicative in any way of its militarisation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the level of arming and equipment of the police in Serbia be completely consistent with the existing legislation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely certain. All of the weaponry and equipment of the police in Serbia was in complete conformity with the relevant legislation. I believe there is a rule book or maybe a provision on the arming of the police. I could add that it is one thing to talk about the weapons that one person may carry and weaponry in the possession of the police force as such. It doesn't mean, by the way, that all the weaponry can be used in every occasion. The fact that the police had a certain amount and quality of weapons does not mean that they are allowed to use it without control. The use of weapons depended on the level of threat and security risk. Of course, weapons are also used as part of police coercion, in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Police coercion, in keeping with the law, you said?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that under tab 8 we can find the rules on the level of arming of authorised officers -- rules on the weapons of authorised officers and employees performing certain duties?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that there is anything in this text that is particularly important that you could quote in corroboration of what you said about the difference between the sidearms of a person, of a particular individual, and the police force as such?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can quote. I know this text. Article 1, paragraph 2, says: "The firearms of authorised officers shall comprise pistols, revolvers, sub-machine-guns, rifles, and light machine-guns. "3. The firearms of employees performing certain duties shall comprise pistols, revolvers and rifles." Therefore, in Article 1, there is a stipulation of the type of weapons to be carried by certain persons such as police officers and employees of the police with certain powers. Article 2 defines the type of weapons that are considered adequate for members of the police. I will quote: "The firearms used by the police, by police units shall comprise machine-guns, mortars, hand-held launchers and rocket launchers, hand grenades, rifle grenades, and other shells and the weapons with which certain police vehicles are equipped." I can thus confirm that the police of Serbia had nothing in its arsenal apart from these specified weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before -- I see before that passage and after that passage there is reference to what's described as chemical weapons. So what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... actually complete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply overlooked that I should read on. So in paragraph 3 of Article 2 we read: "The chemical weapons of police units shall comprise chemical pistols, rifles and adapters for launching chemical and other projectiles and chemical hand grenades, atomisers and devices containing tear gas." Of course the very next paragraph specifies the weapons used by police units for special operations and by special police units. These weapons can also comprise particular kinds of special weapons, cold steel, and weapons with a bowstring.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. I would just like to ask one other question. Does -- does what you have said so far mean that every police officer, every ordinary police officer was authorised to have the weapons which you've outlined; that's the first two categories of weapons, the second paragraph and the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I wasn't clear enough. Article 1, paragraph 2, which I just quoted, refers to every police officer individually, whereas Article 2 in its entirety deals with police units. So what we read in Article 1 is what every police officer has. Of course it doesn't mean that he carries it all all the time he is on duty. Article 2, however, deals with police units; police station, police platoon, police battalion, et cetera, company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the answer is, in fact -- explains it fully but can I just be absolutely clear: That means that where the expression "authorised officials" is used, or "authorised officials and employees," that simply means police officers, anyone who is an authorised police officer. It doesn't mean you need special authority to be specially authorised to carry a weapon of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every police officer always has on him either a pistol or a revolver; as we call them, short barrels. Every policeman also, in case of extraordinary assignments, may have a long barrel on him. Let me be even more precise. In paragraph 2 of Article 1 says that an individual policeman may carry either a pistol or a revolver Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. plus a submachine-gun or a rifle or a light machine-gun. Any other weapon is to be used mainly in emergency extraordinary assignments, such as anti-terrorist activity, but not on regular duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, now in view of these rules and what they contain, and they contain everything referring to weapons used by the police force, General, did you have any comparison as to what the weapons used in other police forces in the world -- or in Europe first and foremost, let's take Europe first. Is there anything there within the weaponry of the police force in Serbia that does not exist in the weaponry of policemen in other European countries, for instance?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course we took that into account, bore it in mind and quite certainly there are no essential differences. The differences are only in type of -- the type or make of weapons but not in the weapons themselves, and of course we also bore in mind the conditions under which certain weapons are used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can that possibly be correct, though, because we know of countries where police officers do not routinely carry weapons at all, and therefore that must be a situation which is entirely different from the situation that you're envisaging in Serbia. So it may be better if you were able to say which countries you were comparing the Serbian position with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Your Honour. So certain countries, of course, even in their regular duties do not carry weapons, but they are exceptions to the best of our knowledge. So we were in a position to analyse the countries surrounding us and we looked at the French police, in actual fact the French police force, and a unit such as the gendarmerie, for example, the Carabinieri units in other countries of Western Europe. They have similar weapons. Of course those weapons cannot be seen publicly in peacetime when they go about their regular duties. They are the types of weapons that are only used when the situation and circumstances merit the use of such weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, but a policeman, an officer on the beat, what kind of weapons do they have?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the Republic of Serbia, it is generally known and specified what a regular police officer carries on a daily basis in Belgrade, for instance. It is a pistol manufactured by the Crvena Zastava factory of Kragujevac, so domestically produced, and none of the rest that I read out. Now, of course if there were any demonstrations, violent demonstrations or others, then the unit would have to carry out an assignment in situations of that kind and such a unit would have some of the other weapons specified, a few chemical substances as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What about a football stadium, a unit providing security for an important football match at a stadium, for example? Would it have any special devices, special weapons?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Let's take the case of football matches which are frequently held in Belgrade. The police also uses the pistol, just that one weapon officially issued service pistol, and in certain conditions chemical weapons with special devices. They would have to wear special uniforms, protective devices, and so on. But for a football match, just the regular service pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, General, in addition to the ranks that you told us about and the organisational aspects of the police force, and we were just looking at weapons, the equipment and training of special units were used as an argument to prove the militarisation of the police force. So not only special purpose units but the entire police force was used to show that there was militarisation of the force. Now, arguments such as this, are they justified, would you say? Or, rather, could you compare the situation from that period of time and the situation in Serbia at present, for example.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, comments of that kind which were based on the type of training and organisation for the special police forces are not an argument in favour of the police's militarisation. It doesn't show that. I'm sure that the organisation, training, equipment of special police units at that time was commensurate to the security threats that the Republic of Serbia had to deal with at that period of time. I'm also certain that most European countries have similar units for similar purposes, for purposes in situations of that kind. And I think your question was also for me to compare the special units then and special units now in Serbia for the same kind of assignments. I can confirm that the present gendarmerie in the Republic of Serbia, which to all intents and purposes was a replacement for the previous special police units, is only an additional better qualified, better organised and equipped force in terms of training, deployment, et cetera. And at that time, we wanted to have the kind of unit that we have today in the gendarmerie of Serbia, for example. And the government of Republic of Serbia never had enough money to put that into effect because professional units for that type of assignment require far greater funds from the budget than the units that were a compromise at the time, the units in force and a compromise and ones that answer to the needs of the situation in Serbia and what Serbia was able to offer and also in respect of the security situation that the country had to face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we were to take the criteria of seeing the degree of militarisation, for instance, what comparison could you make between the special police units at that time and the present gendarmerie?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is incontestable that the present day gendarmerie is far more similar to a military unit than the units of the day. That of course does not mean that I have a negative attitude towards the gendarmerie of the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking of your attitude towards them but I'm asking you from a factual basis in terms of organisation, weaponry, training, and so on and so forth. So that's the terms I wanted you to make the comparison.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these units were serviced by regular policemen whereas the present gendarmerie is a professional unit and is more like, if I can use the term, a standing army than the previous unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Returning to the assignment of ranks, were civilians who worked in the police force also assigned ranks, civilians such as typists and the translators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not. Quite certain that that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, General, in view of the question you were just asked, if an individual had a rank, which -- a person performing some technical duty as was mentioned a moment ago, for example, some administrative work, then what kind of ranks would those be?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ranks, as I've already said, in the police force of Serbia could have been gained by only authorised officers, that is to say policemen, individuals with police authorisation. No administrative workers had police authorisation. They enjoyed the same status as any other employee in the administration of local government or state government, and they couldn't have received a rank of any kind let alone the rank of general. Of course, an exception could have been made in the case of somebody who was an administrative worker who in the course of time became a policeman. But there again, he could have been given the rank which corresponded to his professional training and experience and the time spent on the job at a set post or position. But I don't know of any such cases myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, all right, according to the law, we can see that the ranks refer to authorised officers and not, for instance, drivers, cooks, mechanics, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Administrative staff, you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, administrative staff.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were classical positions and posts just like administrative employees and staff in other ministries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, now since we have followed the logical course of events and arrived at this subject matter, I'd like to ask you something about the special purpose police units and they are otherwise mentioned fairly frequently here with respect to the events in Kosovo. General, at one point in time during one period, as far as I know up to 1996, in fact, you yourself were the commander of special police units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what kind of units they were.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We've already started discussing matters of that kind, but what I could tell you is this: Special police units are police units, as we call them special purpose units, that is to say units intended to perform special assignments of different complexity, levels of complexity. So those units most frequently carry out assignments when those assignments go way beyond the scope and capabilities of the ordinary units, and they are very broad, stemming from an ordinary football match, for example, where it is difficult for the local police force to maintain law and order. Then there can be public meetings and rallies of different types which, in the security related sense, surpass the capabilities of the regular police force, and it can also go towards arresting and taking into custody various individuals, groups, criminals, and it ranges to anti-terrorist assignments. The other thing that is important and that I should like to mention, something we've already touched upon, is this: They are units of provisional -- provisional units, ad hoc units that are established when the need for their involvement arises, and they remain in such a formation for as long as the assignments for which they were formed last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And once that assignment is completed, what happens to that special assignment unit or ad hoc units? What happens?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They go back to their regular duties within the frameworks of their regular police stations. And I'm talking about policemen from all regular units. So patrol policemen on the beat, traffic policemen, border policemen, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So policemen going about their regular duties, when the need arises, when the security situation is such, they are organised and sent to form special police units, ad hoc units for the performance of a set assignment, and they do not exist outside that assignment. They go back to the jobs they were doing beforehand; policemen on the beat, patrol policemen, border policemen, or whatever else they were doing beforehand; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But let me also say that they are organisationally provided for in advance. They're -- the members, the strength and deployment of each unit is decided beforehand but, of course, the number of policemen assigned to a task and unit depends on the situation. Not all the units, the special purpose units, are deployed but only those parts in sufficient numbers to carry out the assignment set.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, tell us, when was the first time, to the best of your knowledge, that these special units were established, special police units? Were there units of that kind in the former Yugoslavia, for example?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a subject I am well-versed in. Those units under a different name did exist in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. Now, the reason for which these units were established in the republics of the former Yugoslavia was one that was very well known. It was the storming of a terrorist group in the Radusa area of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1972, when that incident occurred. And in the clash between the security forces with that particular terrorist group, as I said in 1972, quite a number of policemen and soldiers were killed, fell casualty. And of course this was an event which was very worrying to all the former Yugoslav republics. And as a result of their concern and to counteract a situation of that kind, they decided to set up the special police units in Serbia. So from that day onwards they have existed throughout in Serbia up until the year 2000 or, rather, when the gendarmerie was established. But now they, too, can be revived in Serbia should the need arise, pursuant to certain legal stipulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging by the rules and regulations, General, who has the right to engage special police units?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Special police units were exclusively established by the minister of the interior or the head of the sector for public security pursuant to an order from the minister. The same method is applied, or the same legal basis is applied for their engagement of the special units set up by an act -- a decree of the minister. They too can be deployed only by an activating order from the minister or in certain cases by the head of the public security sector, pursuant to authorisation from the minister once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, take a look at tab 5 of the rules governing the internal organisation of the ministry. I am just going to quote one paragraph from Article 6.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. What number did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is tab 5, and Article 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. They're not translated. You're citing one article, Article 6. Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 6: "In addition to the organisational units established pursuant to these rules for the ministers of the interior for the performance of these duties under Article 2," and those units were listed above, I mentioned the secretariat and the maps, and so on and so forth, it says, "The minister of the interior shall establish a special purpose units of the police force operative groups and other special units." So he exclusively has the right -- these units can exclusively be established and mobilised by the ministry. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And from the text it would emerge that it -- that the minister is the sole person that can do so. But there was another authorisation, that the minister can pass on his authorisations to the heads of sectors, and you can't see this from that article. And then the heads of sectors can proceed according to what is stipulated in this article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained to us how they were formed and sent back to their original jobs. Now, was there any permanence with respect to the composition and deployment of these units?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I answered that question in part as well, because there is never any permanence with respect to the numerical state and organisation of the parts deployed. These units, for the most part, are engaged in smaller sections commensurate with the assignment, and they remain on assignment only while the assignment is in force. So they are usually deployed for brief periods with less members rather than being engaged as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, paragraph 2 of Article 6 that we have on the ELMO says the following: "By the act of forming a special unit pursuant to Article 1 of this -- these regulations, the tasks of the unit is determined, the time period, the authorisations, and other conditions of work of the police units. The units are formed from the members of the ministry, the reserve force members and, when required, persons over the age of 18 who go to military schools." So those are specifications as to the composition and strength of these units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, outside this is it possible to form any unit at all, outside the decision taken by the minister?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the legal framework and grounds for -- on the basis of which these units are established, stipulating the assignments, the time period, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, what about the reserve police force in Kosovo and Metohija? How is that force manned?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the police -- of the reserve police force, their status and the mode of their employment are regulated in the law on internal affairs, and of course I cannot remember the exact article. As for engaging this force in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 - I assume that this is the year you have in mind - and 1999, and generally speaking, for that matter, it was only the reserve force from the local secretariats that were engaged. Engaging the force outside Kosovo was a very sporadic thing. Perhaps there were only a few exceptions. This reserve force in Kosovo and Metohija was primarily engaged in provisional police departments, and they were seconded to regular police units to help them out. Most of the policemen from these regular units were engaged in special police units at the time. So they were practically engaged to replace the active duty officers who were combatting terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, although their functions would be specific, would these special units have powers different from ordinary policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The law on internal affairs, and other laws, of course, define the same powers for all policemen. That is to say, for all authorised officers irrespective of the units that they're on. Of course I'm talking about police authorisation, that is to say the right to ask a person for an ID, to bring a person into custody, and so on and so forth. As for assignments and tasks, of course there are differences, because regular policemen as a rule carry out standard customary police tasks protecting law and order, providing security in particular places, et cetera, whereas special units usually carry out more complex tasks, but they have the same authority and they enforce the same legal regulations when doing their jobs. That is to say that there is no special authority vested in special units. There is authority vested in authorised officers irrespective of the unit that they're in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few moments ago you mentioned that the law on internal affairs regulates this.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I please take this page and put it back into the tab?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the law on internal affairs now. That is tab 1.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few moments ago in response to my questions you explained how the members of the reserve police force in Kosovo and Metohija were engaged and who the members were, and you said that this is regulated in the law on internal affairs. Here you have it from Article 27 onwards. It says the reserve force. 27, 28, 29, and 30. Are these the laws -- the regulations or, rather, the articles of the law that regulate the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be put on the ELMO. It's translated? No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already answered. I explained which tasks the reserve force had, but I did not explain in which way it was engaged. So the reserve force can be engaged only through an order of the minister to engage the reserve force. The authority is similar to that of the authority of the minister to engage special units. Article 27, Article 28, and Article 29 refer to the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I assume that right now we won't be needing the law on internal affairs any longer. There is no need for further comment except for what you've already said just now.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When talking about special police units, you explained who could give them orders, how they were engaged, and so on and so forth. Can you please tell us now more specifically, when there is a particular situation where a special police unit is engaged, under whose command are these engaged parts of police units? You said that certain parts were engaged depending on the need involved. Under whose command are they, then, these individual parts?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Proceeding from the fact that one always engages a certain number of policemen and a profile of policemen that are required in a particular area in order to resolve a particular problem, then that kind of formation and that kind of number of people is sent to that area, in accordance with the actual assignment. Of course, everything happens in a particular territory. In that territory it is always the locally organised unit that is in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be clear: For example, if a special police unit - let's take Kosovo, Pristina or Urosevac -- never mind. Does that mean that this special police unit that came to resolve a particular task is under the command of the head of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs who is locally in charge, either Pristina, Urosevac, or whatever, or the secretariat of the municipality where they came?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Perhaps I didn't understand the previous question very well. For example, if a company of special police units from Kraljevo comes to Belgrade to help the Belgrade SUP in order to provide security for a football match, which is often the case, of course it is the leader of that unit who is in charge of that unit. He came with his unit, but they are placed under the command of the staff that are in charge of the entire security of that football match in Belgrade. So they are resubordinated to the local commander who is in charge of a particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about special police forces and special police units in Kosovo and Metohija, special police units were engaged there for a certain period of time. You explained a few moments ago that a special police unit would be engaged for a particular period of time. How long were special police units usually engaged in Kosovo and Metohija, as a rule?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. Usually parts of special police units that were sent to Kosovo and Metohija were engaged usually for about 40 days. After that period, they would be replaced by other units also from the ranks of special police units. The personnel were particularly established for each case, that is to say their leaders and also the length of their stay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, how many special police forces were there in Serbia at the time that we're talking about here and now, '98 and '99 that is, and what was their establishment structure like?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for numbers of all the special police units, again I would like to remind you of the fact that we have to use this in the plural: Special police units. There are several of them. Their total number was about 15.000. Of course, that number includes about 5.000 members of the reserve force. So the total of active duty officers would be about 10.000. And all these 15.000 members of the active and reserve forces of the police were structured in seven detachments, as we will called them, of the A composition, six were B, and I think seven again were R.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: R being the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, R being the reserve force. Every one of these detachments within their internal organisational structure had companies, and every company had platoons, and every platoon had a squad. That is to say that the organisational structure was quite similar to a military organisational structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, for how many days were people usually engaged in special police units in Kosovo and Metohija during those years, in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean what the total was or how many days it lasted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. For example, say a beat policeman from a town in central Serbia is within a special police unit which was sent to Kosovo and Metohija for a certain amount of time. How long would that unit stay there? How long would that man be kept away from his home and the town where he worked and in this unit? In 1998 and 1999, how long would they usually stay there in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that such units went to Kosovo and Metohija and stayed there for about 40 days on average. After that, they would return to their original units and go on with their regular duties. After a certain amount of time, depending on the necessity involved, they would sent for another 40 days. It would be very hard for me to say now annually how long a particular individual would stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they went for 40-day stints.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then they would go back to their units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the special police unit in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999? How many members of special units were in Kosovo and Metohija altogether? What was their maximum level at a given point in time?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From mid-1998 until mid-1999, the number went up, but as far as I know, on average there were between 3 and 4.000 members of the special police unit. Sometimes there were perhaps even less. The maximum, though, was about 7 or 8.000. So approximately 100 per cent more than the strength of the local police force, and of course this was during the time of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're not going to go back to tab 13 because we've already dealt with these tables and you can see the numerical levels there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, many things could be heard about these special police units, that they were some kind of very special units, very particularly established for engagement in Kosovo and Metohija only. Also, that these were some kind of death-sowing units, punitive units. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what I've already said and what I'll add now, such statements are absolutely nonsensical and incorrect. First of all, special police units cannot belong to very specialised units at all. They cannot be belong to that category. We've already said they basically belong to regular police structures, their personnel belonged to these units and they are engaged temporarily. In addition to that, the assignments are not special assignments. Any police provides security for a public gathering. Any police arrests or brings into custody persons who commit crimes. So the same goes for these units. These units did not undergo specialised training. Of course they had training for the kind of tasks that I've already referred to. Most importantly, these units were certainly not established only for the purpose of going to Kosovo and combatting terrorism there. I've already said that their tradition dates back to 1972 and perhaps even the period before that. I know from 1972 for sure. As for their stay in Kosovo, nobody really wanted them to go to Kosovo and to have to handle the kind of work they did there and that they were faced with. It just so happened that just before the events in Kosovo and during the actual events in Kosovo, these units had to receive additional training in order to be able to deal with that kind of situation and in order to carry out their tasks lawfully and regularly and survive at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 16 -- actually, before that, let's clarify something. On the basis of what you've said, it can be established that special police units do not belong to the category of specialised units.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were not established for the security related events in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say that very categorically?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the core of my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down. It is too fast for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, did you hear that? The interpreters are asking you to slow down, to observe a pause between question and answer. That applies to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't hear the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't either. But I know that, as opposed to the witness, who does not know about that. However, we get carried away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please look at tab 16.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that this document has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this is translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is but one example. It is a decision on the establishment of special police units. It says in the preamble that pursuant to Article 6 on the rules of the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior -- we've just quoted that Article 6 when we looked at the rules on the internal organisation. This is what the minister invokes. And the minister hereby adopts the following decision on the establishment of special police units. And now it says here how they are established and how they function. So paragraph 1, General: "Special police units of the Ministry of the Interior, hereinafter referred to as PJM, shall be established with the overall strength of fifteen police detachments five of which shall be based in Belgrade and two each in Novi Sad, Pristina, Uzice, Kragujevac, and Nis."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the major towns in Serbia and that is where the majority of the police force is. So would that be the reason why they were deployed in this way?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the reason. And also the geographic distribution in part affected this pattern as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on it says that, "The PJM referred to in paragraph 1 of this item at the Secretariat of the Interior shall be from two police platoons up to a detachment in strength, as per the organisational and establishment chart which is attached to this decision and is an integral part of it."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. The organisational structure is further specified in the attachment but I don't believe we have the attachment here. I did explain it, though, when I spoke about the number of detachments and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said seven detachments of the A force, six detachments of the B force, and seven of the reserve force. And we saw in tab 13 each of these things one by one. What is it about this decision that is consistent with the explanations you gave about the organisation and establishment of special police units? What is identical to your explanations?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This decision practically confirms all my previous answers. First of all, we see that this decision was enacted by the minister, late Zoran Sokolovic, and this decision governs all the matters that are to be stipulated by such decision pursuant to the law on the organisation of the ministry. Of course this decision remained in force all the way up to the moment when the gendarmerie was established, and the only change is that the name "milicija" is changed into "policija."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will draw your attention to item 6, which says: "Ministry employees who are members of the PJM shall remain at their posts and perform their regular duties when they are not engaged in the PJM, and shall exercise the rights proceeding from their employment in accordance with their letters of appointment."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a reference to policemen in various workplaces who remain in those workplaces. In the next paragraph, we read: "PJM members are entitled to compensation for engagement in the PJM in accordance with the law and internal ministry rules."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they have some per diem and other payments.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this decision adopted in full conformity with the rules we quoted from earlier?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see here any particular detail that should be clarified with regard to special police units?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Perhaps we can come back to it when we deal with further tabs. What we have here is a document which confirms all my previous answers regarding the establishment of special police units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us look at tab 17 now. This previous decision was adopted by the minister, and under tab 17, we see the decision on the establishment of PJM, signed by assistant minister and head of public security sector Radovan Stojicic, also in 1993. We see that this was addressed to all secretariats from one to 32.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas this particular copy was addressed to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was addressed to what was then called the PJM headquarters in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain. In 1993 there were no particular security problems there, or were there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, but staff of the Ministry of the Interior was operating in Pristina nevertheless. If I didn't mention it earlier, let me say now that beginning with 1990, the ministry staff operated in Pristina up to 1999. Only the personnel changed and the assignments changed. In peacetime -- in more peaceful times, duties were more regular, such as crime prevention and control, whereas in other times such as peaks of crisis it was more oriented towards anti-terrorist activity. If we remember the rules on the establishment of special police units, we see also from this decision the level of management, the level of leadership in the ministry which signs certain enactments and which level determines particular assignments in the establishment of units, in the training of units, writing of particular documents, et cetera. And we see that this document is signed by the head of sector, no lower level officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this para 2, we see an explanation of who is required to give approval for which posts, which positions, and how, beginning with detachment commanders, company commanders, et cetera. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 governs the operation of the existing force. We see that detachment commanders and deputy detachment commanders must be appointed with the approval of the commander of the PJM, whereas, as we see in the next line, detachment command, company commander, and deputy commander can be appointed with the approval of the detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so on. It's always with the approval of the superior commander.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope this is self-explanatory and obvious. We have attachments as well. What is under tab 18? It is entitled "The basic principles for forming special police units of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia." It's a document from the 1st of August, 1993. Explain very briefly what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document provides a basis or guidelines for forming these units, stipulates for which assignments they are formed and in which ways they will be used. This is an enactment, but in actual fact it has the nature of guidelines as an aid to Secretariats of Internal Affairs for them to better understand the way of forming, the purpose, the replenishment and equipment of these units. It was happening at the moment when these units were being formed for the first time, and the secretariats needed to understand their purpose and way of organisation. So this is the purpose of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look now at tab 19. This is a decision to establish the 124th Intervention Brigade of the PJP, special police units. It is a decision of the minister again. I believe there was a question raised earlier on about the nature and place of this Intervention Brigade within the special police units. Can you give us an explanation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see here a decision to establish one of the Intervention Brigades of the PJP, special police units, but it actually refers to the linking of one of the PJP detachments, that is the Kosovo and Metohija detachment, with one of the mechanised units in Pristina. Since these two units merged into one, it was necessary to adopt a decision to rename this 24th Detachment, if I remember correctly, and this mechanised unit, and the newly formed unit was named 124th Intervention Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll take the 20-minute break now. We're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. The microphone is on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please look at tab 20. What can we find there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch dated 8 March 1999, which issues an activating order for certain parts of special police units that are sent to Kosovo and Metohija to replace previously sent parts of special police units. This is consistent with one of my earlier answers to your question about who issues orders to engage PJP, special police units. In this case, this was General Djordjevic who issued this order on the orders of the minister. In this period, Colonel General Vlastimir Djordjevic issued most such orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the fourth paragraph from the top of this dispatch, it says that members of the PJP shall remain on duty there for up to 40 days. That is consistent with what you said about the length of one stint. It says: "Members of the PJP shall remain on assignment for 40 days without the right to leave the unit for the duration of the shift."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This echoes my previous statement that parts of units rather than whole units are deployed. And we can see that from the SUP of Novi Sad Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. only certain companies of certain detachments are sent to this assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the penultimate paragraph. Before that we read: "Members of the PJP shall be relieved of their regular duties by 0700 hours." So they are relieved of their regular duties when they are transferred to special police units?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with what you said about them replacing previously sent units, it says: "For the employees returning from assignment, organise reception, two days off," et cetera, et cetera. Was that the usual practice, to maintain a certain level of presence in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same level of presence was maintained using various units each serving a 40-day stint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the next tab? Is it a similar dispatch, sending a different unit according to the same scheme?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is the same kind of dispatch, sending different units to replace their colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under tab 22, is that the same kind of order?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same scheme, same principle. The only thing that is different is the time and the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says again: "For returning members, organise a reception, two days off," et cetera. We see from this series of dispatches how one and the same level of presence was maintained in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, are we going to deal with the exhibits and their admission later, or shall I tender them in succession, stage by stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: These appear to be amenable to being dealt with at the end, so we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, could you tell me why these dispatches were sent to the principal of the secondary school? That's the school in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's tab 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And 22.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will look, of course, but I suppose that it is the secondary school had a role to play in transportation; to provide buses, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one correction. Maybe it was a mistake in interpretation. It was the secondary school in Sremska Kamenica, not in Mitrovica. The school in Kamenica is the School of Internal Affairs. It is a MUP school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's Mitrovica in tab 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, mine too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will establish easily exactly which school it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, it must be a translation mistake in your copy, because you will see in tab 20 it says secondary school in Sremska Kamenica. Mitrovica is a much better known town, a larger town. Sremska Kamenica is smaller. Maybe the translator made an error. But the police cannot be wrong about their own school; they know it is located in Sremska Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note Kamenica in B/C/S version. It should have been a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a secondary School of Internal Affairs from which, by the way, this general graduated when he was a boy. You heard about that when he was giving us his curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can suppose, although it's difficult to understand from the contents what this is about, this dispatch -- such dispatches are addressed to those parties that are involved in a certain assignment. This can be either a case of the school in Kamenica providing support in some logistical assignments, such as providing buses because schools have buses and secretariats rarely do, or maybe somebody from the personnel of the school was assigned to the force that was being sent. We saw from previous provisions that all kinds of profiles can be involved in a special police unit, and this particular school is in the territory of the Novi Sad municipality, and maybe somebody from this school was a part of the Novi Sad unit. I don't think that this dispatch would be addressed to the school if a unit from Kragujevac was concerned, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we just saw a series of dispatches governing the rotation of such units and determining the actions to be taken in this connection. Give me an answer to this general question: What is the control determined by?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Control is determined by the law on internal affairs governing the entire ministry and its activities, and more specifically by the law on organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have that in the binders.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is governed by particular articles dealing with control within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regardless of which specific articles are concerned, we have the entire rules. What are the most senior posts in the Ministry of the Interior, starting from the minister down to beat policemen, in the entire hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The most senior posts in the ministry are specified precisely by the rules. These posts are minister, heads of sectors, heads of administrations in the MUP and heads of sections within these sectors, then heads of secretariats of internal affairs - we've already explained what secretariats are - heads of internal affairs in municipalities, and commanders of police stations. We could go further down below, but this is the level that is specified by the rules of organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where does an assistant minister fit into that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the minister.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we said earlier today, he fits within the senior level of the ministry. There were six assistant ministers. They can at the same time be leaders but not necessarily. Only heads of sectors are at the same time assistant ministers and leaders. Two of the six have the position of leaders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We also saw in documents earlier the reference to a deputy minister. Where does a deputy minister fit in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A deputy minister, we can say, has a limited leadership role. He is deputy to the minister in the minister's absence or sees to duties based on authorisation from the minister. So in the absence of a minister the deputy minister takes over or carries out duties he is authorised to carry out by the minister. So he is in a leadership position when he is acting as deputy to the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is there only one deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just one. And a number of assistants. Several assistants but just one deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he is superior to the assistants. He's between the minister and the assistant minister. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle that is the case, yes, because he can be authorised by the minister exceptionally whereas the assistants on far rarer occasions, much more exceptional occasions, only if the minister or the deputy minister were absent, in their absence could the assistant step in; otherwise not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, during a state of war were there any changes in the conduct of the police and in the -- how the police was controlled and led? We saw the rules and regulations. Now, in a state of war, were there any changes in the authorisation of the police force and how the police force was led?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In police control and leadership, to all intents and purposes there were no changes with the proclamation of imminent war or danger. All the people in leadership positions remained there, and their authorisation or their remit or their right to control were not changed. Of course, the authorisations of the Ministry of the Interior and the authorised officers in the ministry were changed in part through provisions enacted which were in force during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, was your question directed to the state of war that existed or the typical position in a state of war?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a state of war at all events. But what I wanted to do was to show some documents, which unfortunately we received subsequently, but they are provisions, rules and provisions. So it's not a document that is a report or a brief or information, they are rules and regulations. And I was asking the witness whether during a state of war there were differences in command and control and he said that in control there was no difference but with regard to procedure the procedure was simplified during a state of war, but that is regulated on the basis of rules and regulations once again. I did not receive the documents on time, which of course -- or in good time, which is just a comment and regards my own preparations, but I would like to show -- I think that this is something we can place on the ELMO, on the overhead projector. There are several rules and provisions governing behaviour during a state of war which were passed during or, rather, from the start of the war situation, the state of war, and is linked to this issue, the one that we're discussing. It is not incorporated into the documents found in the tabs because Professor Rakic managed to come by this document only late last night. So these documents are photocopies of the Official Gazette of Yugoslavia and Serbia, that is to say official publications which print rules, laws, et cetera, provisions, and so on. So I'd like to ask the general a few questions in that regard and he can answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in citing all these rules and regulations, don't forget that the important question is whether practice accorded with the norms in those rules and regulations. It's one thing to have the rules and regulations --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- what actually happened is another matter. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. Robinson, I hope you are bearing in mind the fact that -- of course what you say is quite true but it depends on the level, because at a state level, of course, the enactment of provisions and guidelines and so on is standard practice. Now, whether that practice of bringing in provisions and passing provisions, whether that coincides with practice lower down, at a level lower down, is another thing altogether and we'll get to that in due course. But as to what is practice and what are the provisions depends at what level you're asking the question. So this is practice at state level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, I was asking you about what changed, if anything, with respect to the way in which the police went into action during a state of war. Do you know about the provision about the criminal -- criminal proceedings during a state of war enacted by the federal government? Decree.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that decree and certain of its provisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to a regular situation, regular state of affairs, were there any major changes that took place?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Not major changes but concrete changes as far as I remember, specific changes which went to the fact that the officials in conformity with the provision could under extraordinary circumstances undertake investigations of some kind, taking them over from the competence and authority of other organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, here the changes provided for are that the organs of internal affairs can undertake investigations without decisions of the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. And as far as I remember, that amendment also referred to the fact that the organ of the Ministry of the Interior can also keep somebody in custody for a period of up to 30 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the application -- this changed in the application of the ZKP, the law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the provision of the Ministry of the Interior enacted in Serbia during a state of war and referring to a state of war, decree pursuant to the orders of the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that decree as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it raise the authorisations during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Negligibly, as far as I can remember. If I remember correctly, the decree had to do with the effectiveness of the disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to provide you with a set of rules and regulations, provision and decrees, governing the internal affairs organs during a state of war, and they say that the authorised personnel from the ministry can, without a warrant, exercise such functions to take into custody persons whom they suspect of having committed certain acts. So searches without a warrant and so on and so forth. And the provision on ID cards during a state of war. So these are several provisions -- and also which refers to public gathers as well. Anyway, this is a set of provisions which envisage certain changes. Now, these changes, are they geared towards speeding up the process or are they substantive in terms of citizens' rights?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: For example, the decree on domicile, for example, and residence and ID cards, I think that the deadline for which persons can apply or say that they have lost their ID cards has been reduced. And if there are public gatherings taking place, then the person convening public gatherings must seek permission prior to holding the gathering. That was another provision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's take a look at this set of provisions, regulations, which stipulate the changes, and I'd like to ask the usher's help and have this placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. Robinson, that I won't have to hand this in for translation, because on the ELMO you'll see that it is a photocopy taken from the Official Gazette, and I have highlighted several passages which the witness can read out and comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at that, General, please.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Decree on the application of the law of criminal procedure during a state of war." That is the first provision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a federal provision, is it, enacted by the federal government?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And Article 6 para 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the date of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 4th of April, 1999. Of course this is a photocopy of the Official Gazette of the FRY. And the date is here, you can see it for yourselves. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, may we see the passage being quoted, because it's been highlighted, the passage and provision has been highlighted.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We cannot see the entire text, but we can guess what it says. "The organ of the interior can in urgent cases --" it probably says "-- take over -- take on investigative work without the decision of the public --" or, rather, "republican prosecutor." I can't see the left-hand side of the text, it's missing, but I can assume what it says, what the words there are. Now, Article 8 is the next article, and it says: "Detention can be determined by the organ conducting an investigation." Probably it also says, "To undertake certain investigative measures." And then: "The detention set by a public prosecutor or state prosecutor or organ of the Secretariat of the Interior can last up until --" I can't see the number of days here, but as far as I remember, detention up to 30 days, custody up to 30 days. And that is an extension of the authorisations of the organs of the interior, the ones they had. May I go on to the next provision? And the next decree is this -- Thank you. So this is the decree governing internal affairs during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the Republic of Serbia now and what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The date is the 7th of April, 1999. And the article highlighted is Article 4. And it reads as follows: "Authorised personnel of the ministry --" that is the Ministry of the Interior -- "can -- may for security reasons without a search warrant conduct searches of individuals while taking them into custody, while holding them in detention, or while arresting them." Taking them into custody. So the exception there is that a warrant is not necessary in that case. So that was that decree. Now we come to the next decree from the same Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia. It is a decree on citizens' gatherings during a state of war. And Article 2 of that decree says that: "Public gatherings can be convened and held" or, rather, persons can take part in that "having received prior permission from the competent authorities, whether that they take place in a closed premises or outside and regardless of the character of the gathering." So the difference here compared to the previous law, the peacetime law, is that this decree changes the law in that it requires permission by the competent authorities to hold meetings of this kind, and the competent authority in this case is the organ of the Ministry of the Interior. The next decree is the decree on residence, on the residence and domicile of citizens, and there it is just the deadline that has changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The time period, which is shortened.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And that all persons are duty-bound to declare their domicile, and the age is dropped there. So records of domicile, reporting domicile and changes of domicile is a duty that all individuals above the age of 14 are required to comply with. Of course, in the previous law, in the law, the age there was 18. So the age has dropped to 14. And Article 3 is important here. Article 3 reads: "Reporting a domicile or a new address must be done immediately, at the latest within 24 hours upon arrival in a new place of domicile or residence once the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. address has been changed." So it's 24 hours here, whereas the standard regulation was this should be done within a period of eight days. And the last decree has to do with identification papers during a state of war, once again published in the same Official Gazette. Of course, Article 1 always says: "In a state of war, the law governing identification cards holds true unless other provisions state otherwise," which means that the existing law is upheld. Now, Articles 2 and 3 once again have reduced the age level. Here persons required to have IDs are persons over the age of 14. And if an ID is lost or if an individual remains without it, that individual is duty-bound to report the matter within the space of 24 hours. Otherwise, the law provided for a deadline of eight days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, the method of control and leadership in the police, can it be compared to the hierarchy in an army?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: An answer to that question is linked to the question of functional decentralisation in the Ministry of the Interior. Or, rather, in the police force of Serbia, the principle of a duty and implementing that duty pursuant to orders is the subject we're dealing with, and this is differentiated from going about your line of duty without specific orders. I've already stated that the protagonists of carrying out police orders are the policemen themselves and not their leaders. And let me repeat this again: In that sense, political authorisations are the same both for policemen with, say, one year of work experience as they are for the head of a sector, for example. So the principle is the same. All the employees or workers or members of a police force are equated with respect to police authorisation and competency, and that is how we show that the duty to carry out orders is not the overriding principle. And in the police force, it is rarer to follow orders issued by a superior police officer but, rather, it is on the basis of each policeman's duty and to apply the authorisations stipulated by law which relate to each and every policeman individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, are you trying to say that a policeman doesn't have to be ordered to carry out the law? He does directly act in accordance with the law and that is why he is an authorised officer?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Every official acts in accordance with the law, without waiting for any kind of order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all fairness, I didn't have this before, but now I do have it separately. Tab 6. That is to say the rule book on the conduct and interpersonal relations of the employees of internal affairs organs. You explained what the rule was. What happens when there is an order?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: When there is an order, the key principle is the duty to carry out an order. However, this principle has serious constraints. That is to say, the duty to carry out an order does not mean that one is duty-bound to carry out any order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a translation of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If you haven't got it, we'll put it on the ELMO. There aren't too many parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got tab 6?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, regrettably not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to ask the usher to put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just these parts that are highlighted, the second chapter; that is to say, the duty to carry out tasks and orders. So if you look at Article 21, that is what I'd like to have quoted.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my copy, there is only part of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on the next page if --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't got the next page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then I'll give you my page. The duty of carrying out tasks and orders. It starts on one page and then the other articles are on the next page. Could you please just quote what is marked here.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the rules on the conduct and interpersonal relations of employees of internal affairs organs, and this is chapter 2: "The duty to carry out tasks and orders." Article 21: "The head of an organ, the head of a service, organisational unit and unit of the police or an employee who they authorise issue to employees --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It can't be seen now. Yes, now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: " -- oral and written orders to carry out official tasks and duties." Article 22: "An order to exercise authority that is vested by law in authorised officers of an organ can only be issued by an employee who is authorised on the basis of law, regulations passed on the basis of a law, or on the basis of an order of his superior to issue such orders." Article 23: "An order has to be lawful, complete, timely and clear so that the employee concerned can understand it." Article 24: "An order to directly carry out concrete official tasks is as a rule issued to an employee by his immediate superior." And we have explained who their immediate superiors or supervisors are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It can't be seen. Well, now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Article 25: "An employee is duty-bound to carry out all orders issued by the head of the organ or, rather, his immediate supervisor issued in order to carry out service except those ordering the commission of an act which would constitute a crime." Paragraph 2 reads as follows: "If the implementation of an order would constitute a crime, the employee is duty-bound to report this directly to his higher supervisor or the head of the organ."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think that we can move on now. Is there anything specific with regard to the duties of policemen in terms of carrying out the tasks that are strictly related to their working hours, when they are in uniform, or are there any specific characteristics as far as the police is concerned?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is special with regard to policework is the duty of a policeman to carry out certain duties regardless of whether he is on duty or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you concretely: For example, a person is not on duty, he is on vacation, for instance, but he sees the commission of a crime. Is he bound to intervene? Is he duty-bound to intervene?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That kind of thing, like crime control. A policeman is duty-bound to engage in such activities regardless of whether he's on vacation or at home. In addition to that, in the Republic of Serbia it is the duty of a policeman, when carrying out such tasks, it is his duty to expose himself to danger if need be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think we've explained that sufficiently. General, who led the units of the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Regular police units in Kosovo and Metohija were led by their leaders. As for extraordinary units, they were led by persons appointed for that particular purpose under extraordinary circumstances. And specifically as far as, say, combat -- the combat of terrorism is concerned, there was a staff for combatting terrorism that was established in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when was the staff of the Ministry of the Interior for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija established?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC
